misconceptions.statement: Puberty starts just because the body has grown big enough.
misconceptions.why: Students see only the visible growth and not the hidden hormone signals behind it.
misconceptions.fix: Puberty begins when the pituitary gland sends hormone signals that make the testes or ovaries start working.

probe.question: What starts the changes of puberty in a child's body?
probe.wrong_answer: The body simply becomes big enough, so changes begin on their own.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: Every child must start puberty at exactly the same age, and starting early or late means something is wrong.
misconceptions.why: Class textbooks give a typical age range and students treat it as a fixed deadline.
misconceptions.fix: Puberty usually begins between about 10 and 14 years but the exact age varies; early or late within this range is normal.

probe.question: A girl has not started puberty changes at 13 while her friend has. What does this show?
probe.wrong_answer: She must have a health problem since everyone starts at the same age.

misconceptions.root_belief: everyone follows the same fixed schedule

misconceptions.statement: Testosterone is made by the pituitary gland and oestrogen by the uterus.
misconceptions.why: Students link a hormone to the organ it affects or the master gland instead of the gland that makes it.
misconceptions.fix: Testosterone is made in the testes and oestrogen is made in the ovaries; the pituitary only sends signals to them.

probe.question: Which organ makes testosterone in a boy?
probe.wrong_answer: The pituitary gland makes testosterone.

misconceptions.root_belief: the organ that responds also makes it

misconceptions.statement: Only boys' voices change at puberty; a girl's voice stays the same.
misconceptions.why: Boys' voice breaking is dramatic and talked about, while girls' change is small and unnoticed.
misconceptions.fix: The larynx grows in both boys and girls, but it grows much more in boys, so their voice change is more obvious.

probe.question: Does the voice of a girl change during puberty?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only boys' larynx grows so only boys' voices change.

misconceptions.root_belief: only the most noticeable group shows the change

misconceptions.statement: The Adam's apple is the thyroid gland.
misconceptions.why: Both are in the neck and the cartilage of the larynx is also called the thyroid cartilage, so the names get mixed.
misconceptions.fix: The Adam's apple is the front of the larynx, a lump of cartilage; the thyroid gland is a separate hormone gland below it.

probe.question: What is the Adam's apple that boys develop?
probe.wrong_answer: It is the thyroid gland growing bigger.

misconceptions.root_belief: similar names or places mean same thing

misconceptions.statement: Pimples in teenagers are caused only by eating oily food or not washing the face.
misconceptions.why: Parents and advertisements blame food and dirt alone.
misconceptions.fix: Hormones make the oil glands of the skin more active, which blocks pores and causes pimples; keeping clean helps but does not stop the cause.

probe.question: Why do teenagers get pimples?
probe.wrong_answer: Only because they eat oily food and keep the face dirty.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of adolescent health beliefs and health-education surveys

misconceptions.statement: During the growth spurt all body parts grow together at the same rate.
misconceptions.why: Students picture growing as the whole body getting scaled up evenly.
misconceptions.fix: Different parts grow at different times; hands and feet often grow first, and arms and legs before the trunk, so teenagers can look awkward for a while.

probe.question: Why may a teenager's hands and feet look too big for the body?
probe.wrong_answer: This cannot happen because every part grows at the same rate.

misconceptions.root_belief: everything changes together and equally

misconceptions.statement: Menstrual blood is impure blood or waste that the body is throwing out.
misconceptions.why: Students link a discharge from the body with excretion of waste.
misconceptions.fix: It is the extra lining of the uterus with some blood, prepared for a possible embryo and shed when no egg is fertilised; it is not waste or dirty blood.

probe.question: What is the blood that comes out during a period?
probe.wrong_answer: Impure blood that the body is removing as waste.

misconceptions.root_belief: anything leaving the body is waste
misconceptions.source_hint: surveys and studies on menstrual beliefs among adolescent girls in India

misconceptions.statement: Menstruation is the release of the egg from the ovary.
misconceptions.why: Both happen in the same cycle and are taught close together.
misconceptions.fix: Menstruation is the shedding of the uterine lining; the release of the egg is ovulation, which happens about two weeks earlier.

probe.question: What is happening in the body when a girl menstruates?
probe.wrong_answer: An egg is released from the ovary.

misconceptions.root_belief: linked processes are the same process

misconceptions.statement: A girl loses litres of blood in each period, which makes her very weak.
misconceptions.why: Bleeding for several days looks like a huge amount, and people link it to weakness.
misconceptions.fix: The total fluid lost in a period is small, usually only a few spoonfuls of blood with tissue, so a healthy girl is not made weak by it.

probe.question: About how much blood does a girl lose in one period?
probe.wrong_answer: Several litres, so she should rest completely.

misconceptions.root_belief: dramatic looking means large quantity

misconceptions.statement: The egg is released from the ovary on the days a girl is bleeding.
misconceptions.why: Students take the bleeding, the only visible sign, as the start of the cycle events.
misconceptions.fix: The egg is released about midway through the cycle, around day 14, well after bleeding has ended.

probe.question: When in the cycle is the egg released from the ovary?
probe.wrong_answer: During the days of bleeding at the start of the cycle.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: A normal menstrual cycle is exactly 28 days every month, and anything else means disease.
misconceptions.why: The 28-day figure is given in books as one example and remembered as a rule.
misconceptions.fix: 28 days is only an average; cycles vary and are often irregular in the first years after periods begin.

probe.question: A girl's cycle is 32 days long and sometimes changes. What is true?
probe.wrong_answer: It is abnormal because a normal cycle is always exactly 28 days.

misconceptions.root_belief: everyone follows the same fixed schedule

misconceptions.statement: Periods continue as usual during pregnancy.
misconceptions.why: Students think the body keeps its monthly routine whatever else happens.
misconceptions.fix: After fertilisation the embryo settles in the uterine lining, which is kept, so menstruation stops during pregnancy.

probe.question: What happens to periods when a woman is pregnant?
probe.wrong_answer: They continue every month as before.

misconceptions.root_belief: body processes keep running unchanged

misconceptions.statement: A girl having her period is impure and should not enter the kitchen or a temple.
misconceptions.why: Family customs and taboos are repeated as facts from childhood.
misconceptions.fix: Menstruation is a normal body process, so a girl is not impure; she can do all usual activities, with the hygiene care needed.

probe.question: Should a girl on her period stay away from kitchen and puja room?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, she is impure during her period.

misconceptions.root_belief: what custom practises must be scientifically true
misconceptions.source_hint: sociological and public-health studies on menstrual taboos in India

misconceptions.statement: Menstruation is a disease or illness that needs treatment.
misconceptions.why: Pain, cramps and bleeding feel like being unwell.
misconceptions.fix: Menstruation is a natural part of growing up in girls; only very painful or unusual periods need a doctor's advice.

probe.question: Is menstruation a disease?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, bleeding every month is an illness and needs medicine.

misconceptions.root_belief: unusual body process means sickness

misconceptions.statement: A sanitary pad can be worn all day until it is completely soaked, and that is safe.
misconceptions.why: Germs cannot be seen, so students judge only by how the pad looks.
misconceptions.fix: Pads or cloth should be changed every few hours, even when not full, to prevent germs and infection, and the body should be washed.

probe.question: How often should a pad be changed?
probe.wrong_answer: Only when it is completely full of blood.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: school health and menstrual hygiene management surveys

misconceptions.statement: Whether a baby is a boy or a girl is decided by the mother.
misconceptions.why: The mother carries and gives birth to the baby, so people think she controls everything.
misconceptions.fix: The egg always has an X chromosome; the father's sperm carries X or Y, and it decides the baby's sex.

probe.question: Who decides whether a baby is a boy or a girl?
probe.wrong_answer: The mother decides it.

misconceptions.root_belief: the one who does more decides the outcome
misconceptions.source_hint: documented social and student beliefs about sex determination

misconceptions.statement: A mother's egg can carry either an X or a Y chromosome.
misconceptions.why: Students assume both parents give the same kinds of cells.
misconceptions.fix: Every egg carries only an X chromosome; only sperm can carry a Y, so a Y sperm gives a boy and an X sperm gives a girl.

probe.question: Which sex chromosomes can be present in an egg?
probe.wrong_answer: Either X or Y.

misconceptions.root_belief: both parents give identical contributions

misconceptions.statement: Goitre is caused by eating too much iodised salt.
misconceptions.why: A swollen neck looks like too much of something, and people hear much about salt.
misconceptions.fix: Goitre is a swelling of the thyroid gland caused by lack of iodine, which the gland needs to make thyroxine; iodised salt prevents it.

probe.question: What causes goitre?
probe.wrong_answer: Too much iodine from iodised salt.

misconceptions.root_belief: swelling means too much of something

misconceptions.statement: In danger, adrenaline slows the heartbeat to keep us calm.
misconceptions.why: Students think the sensible reaction to danger is to stay calm and save energy.
misconceptions.fix: Adrenaline makes the heart beat faster, breathing quicker and sends more blood to muscles to prepare to fight or run.

probe.question: What does adrenaline do to the heartbeat when we are scared?
probe.wrong_answer: It slows the heartbeat so we stay calm.

misconceptions.root_belief: the sensible-sounding reaction is the real one

misconceptions.statement: Hormones travel through the nerves like electrical signals.
misconceptions.why: Students know the nervous system sends messages and assume all messages use nerves.
misconceptions.fix: Hormones are made by glands and carried by the blood to the target organs, usually acting more slowly than nerve signals.

probe.question: How do hormones reach the organ they act on?
probe.wrong_answer: They travel along nerves.

misconceptions.root_belief: all body messages travel the same way
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student ideas about the endocrine and nervous systems

misconceptions.statement: Eating only protein foods like milk and eggs is enough for a growing teenager.
misconceptions.why: Protein is called the body-building food, so students think it alone is enough.
misconceptions.fix: Teenagers need a balanced diet with carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins and minerals such as iron and calcium, as well as water.

probe.question: What should a teenager eat for good growth?
probe.wrong_answer: Only protein foods like eggs and milk.

misconceptions.root_belief: one key item is all that matters

misconceptions.statement: Girls need less food and nutrition than boys during puberty.
misconceptions.why: Cultural habits and the idea of small girls lead to giving them less food.
misconceptions.fix: Both need a balanced diet; girls especially need iron-rich food because blood is lost in menstruation.

probe.question: Which teenagers need more iron-rich food?
probe.wrong_answer: Boys, since girls should eat less.

misconceptions.root_belief: need is decided by looks or gender
misconceptions.source_hint: nutrition surveys of adolescent girls in India

misconceptions.statement: Moodiness and irritability in teenagers is just bad behaviour that they choose.
misconceptions.why: Adults only see the behaviour and not the hormone changes and stress behind it.
misconceptions.fix: Hormone changes and new pressures cause mood swings; talking to trusted people, exercise, sleep and a good diet help.

probe.question: Why do teenagers often have sudden mood changes?
probe.wrong_answer: They are being badly behaved on purpose.

misconceptions.root_belief: behaviour is a choice, not body chemistry
